findings.headline: Number of EHCPs forecast to rise about 20% in 2026-27 to around 9,954, after a 25% increase since January 2025
findings.detail: The paper says EHCP numbers are a significant driver of demand and deficit growth. Its SEND Reform Plan aims to shift more children into local specialist provision.
findings.matters: EHCP growth is the underlying driver of the High Needs deficit that many councils and lenders are tracking.
findings.figures: 8,490 EHCPs at 30 September 2026; 1,622 (25%) increase since January 2025; around 20% growth in 2026-27; approximately 9,954 by year end
findings.quote: an increase of 1,622, or 25%, since January 2025

findings.headline: Traded services forecast a gross surplus of £3.307m, £0.167m above the year-end target of £3.140m
findings.detail: The paper says the forecast is marginally lower than Quarter 1, which was £3.390m, but still above target.
findings.matters: A traded surplus above target is an income line that offsets part of the general fund pressure.
findings.figures: £3.307m gross surplus forecast at Q2; £3.140m year-end target; £0.167m improvement on target; £3.390m at Q1
findings.quote: a £0.167m improvement on the year-end target of £3.140m

findings.headline: £1.000m pressure bid submitted for Waste Management through the 2027-28 MTFS refresh
findings.detail: Waste Management is the main pressure in Infrastructure, Planning and Environment, with a remaining service overspend of £1.158m. The paper says cost inflation and tonnage growth cannot be fully mitigated in-year.
findings.matters: A waste disposal overspend carried into the MTFS is a pressure that peers with similar contract exposure will recognise.
findings.figures: £1.000m pressure bid; £1.158m remaining service overspend (4.6%); £1.498m before earmarked reserve movements
findings.quote: a £1.000m pressure bid has been submitted through the 2027-28 MTFS refresh

findings.headline: Spending controls first introduced in 2024-25 will remain in place while a net overspend is forecast
findings.detail: The paper says the controls will be kept under review. It also says the council will avoid new recurring commitments that could constrain future options.
findings.matters: A council keeping spending controls in place until the net overspend ends is a governance signal that peers may compare against their own controls.
findings.figures: spending controls introduced in 2024-25
findings.quote: the spending controls first introduced in 2024-25 will remain in place while a net overspend is forecast

findings.headline: Council says the government is 'minded to proceed' with a two unitary model for Warwickshire, extending the period of reorganisation support
findings.detail: The paper says the government paused and reviewed the Local Government Reorganisation programme. It says the period over which programme, legal, finance and workforce support is needed will be extended, and efficiencies may be delayed.
findings.matters: A council whose reorganisation timetable has moved, and whose savings may be delayed as a result, is a planning risk for lenders and peers in the same position.
findings.figures: two unitary model
findings.quote: the government is minded to proceed with a two unitary model for Warwickshire

findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision forecast to underspend by £1.050m in 2026-27 because the 2025-26 Capital Financing Requirement closed lower than budgeted
findings.detail: The paper says the lower closing requirement reflects significant capital programme reprofiling, particularly within Education and Highways, which reduced the need to finance 2025-26 capital expenditure from borrowing.
findings.matters: A lower CFR and lower MRP tie capital reprofiling directly to revenue borrowing costs, which is what treasury teams compare across councils.
findings.figures: £1.050m MRP underspend; lower closing 2025-26 Capital Financing Requirement than the budget projection
findings.quote: is forecast to underspend by £1.050m in 2026-27 because the closing 2025-26 Capital Financing Requirement was lower than the projection used when the budget was set

findings.headline: Liquidity risk flagged as uncertain timing of the DSG High Needs Stability Grant and other future receipts
findings.detail: The paper lists current liquidity risk alongside fluctuating investment returns and the ongoing cash requirement for forecast deficits. It also notes that capital receipts timing could bring forward external borrowing.
findings.matters: Liquidity risk tied to a single large grant is what lenders and treasury teams will want to understand in the council's cash forecast.
findings.figures: £135.277m HNSG expected 30 November (from section 2.11)
findings.quote: current liquidity risk, reflecting uncertainty over the timing of the DSG High Needs Stability Grant

findings.headline: Residual Transport and Economy underspend of £2.289m, mainly from Home to School Transport
findings.detail: The paper says the underspend is improved by £0.913m since Quarter 1 and should be treated cautiously until remaining contracts are finalised. It names SEN transport as the most uncertain area.
findings.matters: Home to school transport is a rising cost area for many councils, so peers will want to see how a forecast underspend holds once contracts are finalised.
findings.figures: £2.289m remaining service underspend (3.0% of net revenue budget); £0.913m improvement since Quarter 1
findings.quote: After these movements, the remaining service underspend is £2.289m, an improvement of £0.913m since Quarter 1.

findings.headline: Lighthorne Heath Primary School start on site moved to 2027 after a two-year delay, with cost increases
findings.detail: The paper says construction cost inflation and wider site infrastructure allowances have increased the cost, which is £1.496m higher in-year. A request for additional funding is due to be considered by Cabinet in December.
findings.matters: A scheme seeking additional funding after a multi-year delay is the sort of capital risk that finance directors monitor closely.
findings.figures: two-year delay; start on site now in 2027; £1.496m higher in-year spend
findings.quote: A two-year delay due to issues with the wider infrastructure at the site means the anticipated start on site is now in 2027.

findings.headline: Controllable capital programme across all years forecast at £375.766m against an approved budget of £365.366m, a £10.399m overspend
findings.detail: The paper says the overspend is spread across Highways and Education Services. Schemes at an early design stage remain exposed to inflation, and the council will consider whether they should proceed, be reduced in scope or be discontinued.
findings.matters: A multi-year overspend on the controllable programme is what lenders and peers will assess when reviewing capital governance and inflation exposure.
findings.figures: £375.766m all-years forecast; £365.366m approved budget; £10.399m net overspend; Highways £10.686m overspend; Education Services £7.309m overspend
findings.quote: this results in a net forecast overspend of £10.399m across the controllable capital programme

findings.headline: £28.345m of forecast capital spend moved from 2026-27 into future years
findings.detail: The paper says this reflects further changes in project timing since Quarter 1, and that additional reprofiling is likely at Quarter 3. Most of the variance relates to corporate schemes and S278 works.
findings.matters: A large in-year reprofile signals timing risk on capital schemes and the financing needed in future years.
findings.figures: £28.345m reprofiled from 2026-27; £260.680m total approved budget; £232.336m total forecast; £21.802m WCC programme variance; £6.543m S278 variance
findings.quote: note and approve the total movement in the forecast spend on the capital programme of £28.345m from 2026-27 into future years

findings.headline: Controllable capital programme forecast at £203.249m for 2026-27, £0.466m (0.2%) below the approved budget
findings.detail: The paper says most of the total capital variance sits outside the controllable programme, in Warwickshire Investment Fund, WPDG and Asset Replacement Fund schemes and in S278 funded works.
findings.matters: Close alignment between forecast and budget in the controllable programme is a sign of delivery that lenders and peers look for.
findings.figures: £203.249m forecast; £203.715m approved budget; £0.466m (-0.2%) variance
findings.quote: the variance on the controllable capital programme is £0.466m

findings.headline: Pay award of 3.3% forecast to overspend by £0.850m, reduced to £0.550m in year through time-limited underspends
findings.detail: The approved 2026/27 budget held a provision for a 3.0% pay award. The paper says the ongoing budget shortfall will be addressed in the 2027/28 budget setting process.
findings.matters: A pay award above budgeted provision is a cost any council in England will have faced, and how it was closed in-year is comparable across peers.
findings.figures: 3.3% pay award; 3.0% budgeted provision; £0.850m overspend before mitigation; £0.550m in-year overspend after time-limited underspends
findings.quote: Various time limited underspends have been identified and utilised to reduce the overspend to £0.550m in year

findings.headline: The £11.199m residual overspend would be funded from the Short-Term Financial Risk Reserve, using 50% of its £22.408m balance in 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper says this applies if the position is unchanged by year end after mitigating actions. It also says the reserve's use is part of a wider challenge to the MTFS.
findings.matters: The rate at which a council draws down its general risk reserve is a direct signal of its remaining financial headroom.
findings.figures: £22.408m Short-Term Financial Risk Reserve available funds; 50% use in 2026/27; £11.199m residual overspend
findings.quote: funded from available funds of £22.408m in the Short-Term Financial Risk Reserve

findings.headline: Residual overspend of £11.199m compares with unfunded pressures of £6.2m advised when the 2026/27 budget was set
findings.detail: The paper says the residual overspend, after investment fund and earmarked reserve movements, is within the ±2% tolerance at 1.6% of the approved budget. It also says the position does not remove the underlying demand and cost pressures in the MTFS.
findings.matters: A deterioration from the known budget risk, measured against a tolerance, is what finance directors will weigh when judging whether a council's control framework is holding.
findings.figures: £11.199m residual overspend (1.6% of approved budget); £6.2m unfunded pressures at budget setting; ±2% tolerance
findings.quote: members were advised that there were unfunded pressures of £6.2m, so this position has deteriorated from the known risk when the budget was set

findings.headline: Social Care and Support remaining service overspend of £2.988m, with Older People's services at £3.721m
findings.detail: The paper attributes the largest pressure to Older People's services, driven by residential care and a 3% increase in individuals drawing on support. It says the directorate is partly mitigated by a £1.521m underspend in Integrated Care Services.
findings.matters: Adult social care demand growth is a common pressure across English councils, and the paper ties it to the savings plan.
findings.figures: £2.988m remaining service overspend (1.1% of net revenue budget); £3.721m Older People overspend; £1.762m residential care; £1.521m Integrated Care Services underspend
findings.quote: Remaining service overspend £2.988m, 1.1% of net revenue budget.

findings.headline: £26.663m (96.7%) of the £27.579m 2026-27 savings target forecast to be delivered
findings.detail: The paper says a further £2.516m is forecast to be delivered but remains high risk. The largest element is £2.072m for Management of Care Demand within Social Care and Support, where growth in demand threatens delivery.
findings.matters: A finance director will compare the 96.7% delivery rate with the high-risk element still to land.
findings.figures: £26.663m (96.7%) forecast delivery; £27.579m target across 68 initiatives; £916k (3.32%) not delivered; £2.516m high risk; £2.072m Management of Care Demand
findings.quote: £26.663m (96.7%) is forecast to be delivered in line with the plan

findings.headline: £0.916m of savings forecast not to be delivered, all within Children and Families
findings.detail: The shortfall is made up of £0.445m from reducing residential and fostering costs through council foster carers, £0.200m from additional NHS contributions, £0.100m from House Project expansion and £0.171m from staffing reductions or alternative grant funding. The paper says delivery of the fostering saving remains challenging.
findings.matters: A non-delivery figure this size, coming from demand-led children's savings, is the kind of gap peers face when placement savings do not land.
findings.figures: £0.916m (3.32%) savings forecast not to be delivered; £0.445m fostering; £0.200m NHS contributions; £0.100m House Project; £0.171m staffing
findings.quote: The £0.916m forecast savings shortfall relates entirely to Children and Families

findings.headline: Internal fostering placement weeks forecast 3.8% higher than 2025-26, with a £0.352m underspend
findings.detail: The paper describes this as an encouraging shift toward the council's more cost-effective internal provision. It is partly offset by an external fostering overspend of £0.755m.
findings.matters: Shifting placements from external to in-house fostering is a cost lever that peers are also pursuing.
findings.figures: £0.352m internal fostering underspend; 601 placement weeks, or 3.8%, higher than 2025-26; £0.755m external fostering overspend
findings.quote: a £0.352m underspend in internal fostering, where placement weeks are 601, or 3.8%, higher than in 2025-26

findings.headline: Residential placement weeks forecast at 6,780 in 2026-27, up from 6,153 in 2025-26
findings.detail: The paper says the average weekly unit cost increased 5.85%, taking the average annual residential placement cost to approximately £0.379m. This results in a forecast residential care overspend of £9.317m at Quarter 2.
findings.matters: Placement volume and unit cost growth drive the children's services overspend and are the main levers the savings plan depends on.
findings.figures: 6,780 forecast residential placement weeks; 6,153 in 2025-26; 10.2% increase; £7,273 average weekly unit cost; £0.379m average annual cost; £9.317m residential overspend
findings.quote: The service is forecasting 6,780 residential placement weeks in 2026-27, compared with 6,153 in 2025-26

findings.headline: Remaining Children and Families service overspend forecast at £12.326m, 9.0% of its net revenue budget
findings.detail: The paper attributes the overspend mainly to children in care placements, with residential placements the largest driver. Forecast residential placement weeks are up 10.2% on 2025-26, and the average weekly unit cost has risen 5.85%.
findings.matters: Children's residential placement costs are one of the largest non-DSG pressures facing councils nationally, so peers will compare unit costs and volumes.
findings.figures: £12.326m remaining service overspend; 9.0% of net revenue budget; £14.513m gross service variance; 6,780 residential placement weeks vs 6,153 in 2025-26; unit cost £6,871 to £7,273
findings.quote: Remaining service overspend £12.326m, 9.0% of net revenue budget.

findings.headline: Initial review suggests the 2026/27 borrowing requirement is lower than budgeted, with very likely no additional external borrowing
findings.detail: The review covers the HNSG position, pace of the capital programme, balance sheet cash movements and interest rate and local authority lending market projections. The paper says further revenue benefit could be confirmed at Quarter 3.
findings.matters: A council that expects no new external borrowing in the year is a signal to lenders and to peers managing the same cash-flow pressures from the DSG deficit.
findings.figures: No additional external borrowing very likely in 2026/27
findings.quote: Initial findings from the review are suggesting the borrowing requirement for 2026/27 is lower than budgeted for

findings.headline: Cumulative financing cost of the DSG deficit is forecast at £7.9m by the end of 2026-27, rising to £16.4m by 31 March 2028
findings.detail: The paper says the cost is net of the HNSG and is being reflected in the 2027-32 MTFS refresh. It also says these costs are roughly equivalent to a 2% to 4% council tax increase.
findings.matters: This converts the DSG deficit into a General Fund cost, showing how the statutory override moves it onto the council's financing position.
findings.figures: £7.9m cumulative financing cost at end of 2026-27 (net of HNSG); £16.4m by 31 March 2028; roughly 2% to 4% council tax increase
findings.quote: The associated cumulative financing cost has risen to £7.9m by the end of 2026-27 (net of the HNSG)

findings.headline: Council says further DSG support for 2026-27 and 2027-28 deficits is anticipated but unconfirmed, with no allowance in the MTFS
findings.detail: The paper says the amount and timing of further support have not been confirmed. If Government funding does not fully cover the in-year deficit, a pressure of around £25.501m could fall to the MTFS, which the £57.5m Corporate Financial Risk Reserve partly covers.
findings.matters: A council carrying a large unfunded DSG exposure in its MTFS will be watched for how it treats unconfirmed government support.
findings.figures: £25.501m potential pressure if 90% of the 2026-27 in-year deficit is funded; £57.5m Corporate Financial Risk Reserve
findings.quote: Further support is anticipated for deficits arising in 2026-27 and 2027-28, but the amount and timing have not yet been confirmed, and no allowance has been included in the MTFS.

findings.headline: The cumulative High Needs deficit is forecast to rise from £161.498m at 31 March 2026 to £267.264m by 31 March 2027
findings.detail: The paper says the deficit could reach around £385m by the time the statutory override ends on 31 March 2028, before any Government support.
findings.matters: The trajectory toward the override end date is the central risk that peer councils and lenders will be tracking.
findings.figures: £161.498m at 31 March 2026; £267.264m forecast at 31 March 2027; around £385m by 31 March 2028 (before Government support)
findings.quote: The cumulative High Needs deficit was £161.498m at 31 March 2026 and is forecast to increase to £267.264m by 31 March 2027.

findings.headline: £135.277m High Needs Stability Grant confirmed for 2026-27, expected to be paid on 30 November
findings.detail: The grant is 90% of the eligible net DSG deficit at 31 March 2026. The paper says it relates to expenditure already incurred, will be held in a separate earmarked reserve until 31 March 2028, and is not additional funding for wider services.
findings.matters: The size and timing of this grant set how much cash the council must find for the DSG deficit, which is why the paper flags liquidity risk.
findings.figures: £135.277m High Needs Stability Grant; 90% of eligible net DSG deficit at 31 March 2026; payment expected 30 November
findings.quote: the Council has received confirmation of a £135.277m High Needs Stability Grant in 2026-27, expected to be paid on 30 November

findings.headline: The High Needs Block is forecast to overspend by £105.767m in 2026-27, within a net DSG overspend of £104.705m
findings.detail: The paper says the DSG overspend will be held in a negative reserve under the statutory override rather than funded from general resources. The High Needs forecast is up from an initial MTFS planning assumption of £80m.
findings.matters: A finance director here or elsewhere needs to know the size of the in-year DSG overspend that the statutory override is absorbing.
findings.figures: £105.767m High Needs Block overspend; £104.705m net DSG overspend; £80m initial MTFS planning assumption
findings.quote: The High Needs Block is forecast to overspend by £105.767m in 2026-27, contributing to a net DSG overspend across all four blocks of £104.705m.

findings.headline: A Local Government Association financial diagnostic peer review of the council's approach to homes for children in care is to be conducted.
findings.detail: The Children & Families commentary says the LGA will conduct a financial diagnostic peer review specifically considering the council's approach to homes for children in care. The commentary lists this among the actions being taken to address the overspend.
findings.matters: An external financial diagnostic of residential placements is a governance step other councils with similar overspends have used, and its findings will be visible to peers and lenders.

findings.quote: A Local Government Association will conduct a financial diagnostic peer review

findings.matters: A council moving from overspend to underspend on its own homes, while external placements still overspend, shows a shift in cost mix that peers planning in-house provision will want to track.

findings.matters: Falling care numbers combined with a rising residential share is a cost mix pattern that finance directors compare when judging whether demand reductions translate into lower spend.

findings.matters: A High Needs variance of this scale against the grant funding base is a large unfunded cost that other councils and lenders track closely as part of the DSG deficit position.

findings.matters: A reduction in a headline overspend between quarters, shown with the reserve-funded element separated, is a trend that a finance director at another council can compare with their own non-DSG education position.

findings.detail: The Children & Families commentary says Youth Justice remand placements have deteriorated significantly since budget setting, and are now forecast to overspend. The commentary states that part of this is being met from reserves.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Half Year Update Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Liability benchmark shows new external borrowing of £105.0m in 2027/28, rising to £167.0m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The paper says the liability benchmark indicates additional external borrowing is likely in the medium term. It notes the timing and scale depend on capital programme delivery, reserve and working capital movements, and the timing and value of High Needs Stability Grant receipts. It also records that gross debt is forecast to rise from 2027/28, to £341.2m against £236.2m in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A council forecasting a rising need for external debt from 2027/28 will be looking for PWLB or market funding, and the dependence on uncertain DSG grant receipts is a factor peers will recognise.
findings.figures: Total new external borrowing required £105.0m in 2027/28 and £167.0m in 2030/31; gross debt £341.2m in 2027/28 against £236.2m in 2026/27; gross debt 46% of net service expenditure in 2027/28
findings.quote: The liability benchmark indicates that additional external borrowing is likely to be required over the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Half Year Update Report 2026-27
findings.headline: PWLB certainty rates rose across all major maturity brackets in the first half, with 10-year rates going from 5.62% to 6.17%
findings.detail: The paper reports that PWLB rates escalated over the half-year. It states the existing debt portfolio has a weighted average rate of 5.23%, so new external borrowing at current rates would increase overall borrowing cost. It also notes that early repayment of PWLB loans may give discounts and short-term savings, which must be weighed against the risk of higher replacement borrowing later.
findings.matters: Councils considering whether to borrow now or repay early can compare their own portfolio rate and the cost of replacement funding against the PWLB movement the paper records.
findings.figures: 10-year 5.62% to 6.17%; 20-year 6.13% to 6.61%; 50-year 6.01% to 6.37%; existing portfolio weighted average 5.23%; short-term local authority rates 3.8% to 5.5%
findings.quote: PWLB certainty rates escalated across all major maturity brackets over the course of the first half.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Half Year Update Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Total investments fell £54.3m to £117.1m in the first half, with the SEND deficit cited as the main driver
findings.detail: The paper says the reduction in cash equivalents was caused by the SEND deficit, with short-term placements also falling. Liquid funds averaged £124m during the half-year and fell to £67.5m at 30 September, partly due to salary increment back-pay and the timing of large payments. The net borrowing position rose from £64.8m to £119.1m.
findings.matters: A fall in cash and rise in net borrowing while external debt stays flat shows how the DSG deficit is being funded from the council's own cash, which other councils with high-needs deficits will recognise.
findings.figures: Investments down £54.3m to £117.1m; liquid funds average £124m; liquid funds £67.5m at 30 September; SEND cash equivalent movement -£44.1m; net borrowing £64.8m to £119.1m
findings.quote: Total investments decreased by £54.3m to a closing balance of £117.1m, driven by reductions in cash equivalents caused by the SEND deficit (-44.1m)

findings.matters: Peers and lenders can see how a council's SEND-related DSG deficit is growing and how much of it is expected to be funded, which determines the internal resources left to finance the capital programme.

findings.detail: The fund requires three new pension officers and one assistant (£169k) for business-as-usual demand, a governance officer (£45k) for compliance reforms, and a project manager (£58k) for coordination of governance reforms, LGR, and administration projects. These are flagged as new costs over existing commitments.
findings.matters: New recurring staffing costs either drain the pension fund reserves or require increased employer contributions from the council, affecting its general fund budget.
findings.quote: Administration Team 3 Pension Officers and 1 Pension Assistant to meet underlying business as usual demand levels: £169k. Governance Officer post to support growth in governance demands (General Code of Practice, Fit for the Future reforms): £45k.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 for Pension Fund Governance Report
findings.headline: Fund can recover administration costs from employers for late contributions (£500 plus interest) and late data submissions
findings.detail: Under LGPS Regulation 70, the Fund can charge employers for poor performance including late contributions (£500 per occurrence plus 1% above base rate interest), late data submissions (£1,000 plus £100 per week), and persistent data quality problems (£50 per case). The Fund also recharges any Pensions Regulator or Pensions Ombudsman fines in full to the responsible employer. Improvement notices must be issued before enforcement.
findings.matters: These cost recovery powers indicate the Fund has formal enforcement mechanisms for employer compliance. For councils with governance weaknesses or cash flow problems, such charges could represent material unforeseen costs.
findings.figures: £500 per late contribution plus interest; £1,000 plus £100/week for late year-end returns; £50 plus £50/month for late starter information.
findings.quote: Where a serious or persistent and on-going failure to deliver employer responsibilities to the Fund occurs (for example late contributions, late data submissions, or poor data quality), and no improvement is demonstrated by an Employer the Fund may recover costs from an Employer.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 for Pension Fund Governance Report
findings.headline: The Fund is undertaking a formal three-year data cleansing programme to address identified data quality problems.
findings.detail: The Fund acknowledges data quality issues affecting active and deferred members and has commissioned a three-year data cleansing contract. The Fund also operates tolerance policies (e.g., only recalculating deferred benefits if pay changed by more than £250) and uses 'best endeavours' methods including national datasets and insurance database to calculate missing data. This suggests accumulated data accuracy problems that require formal remediation.
findings.matters: Data quality weaknesses in pension administration can result in incorrect benefit calculations, overpayments, member disputes, and regulatory fines. The need for formal remediation indicates past control failures in data governance.
findings.figures: Three-year contract; £250 tolerance threshold for benefit recalculation.
findings.quote: The Fund are entering a three-year data cleansing contract which will allow checks of data on both active and deferred members.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 for Pension Fund Governance Report
findings.headline: Councillors and mayors became LGPS members on 11 May 2026, creating new pension liabilities and contribution obligations.
findings.detail: The LGPS (Amendment) (Elected Member Pensions) Regulations 2026 allow councils to enrol councillors and mayors as scheme members. Councillors must opt in rather than be auto-enrolled, cannot do flexible retirement, and have restricted transfer-in and additional pension rights compared to regular employees. This creates new unfunded pension liabilities for all councils, with mandatory employer contribution obligations for any councillor who joins.
findings.matters: A new employee pension scheme creates additional unfunded liabilities affecting councils' balance sheets and ongoing contribution rates. For a lender, this is a material change to the cost base of English local government.
findings.figures: Councillor scheme came into force 11 May 2026.
findings.quote: Following the LGPS (Amendment) (Elected Member Pensions) Regulations 2026 coming into force on 11 May 2026, councillors and mayors in England are eligible to join the LGPS.

findings.headline: Governance failure risk score 16 now explicitly flags potential for non-pension objectives imposed on LGPS funds
findings.detail: The fund maintains governance failure as its second-highest-rated risk (score 16, unchanged from June 2026). The risk register now explicitly cites the potential for LGPS funds to be assigned additional objectives beyond paying pensions to members. This reflects regulatory and political pressure on pension funds to support local objectives (e.g., investment mandates, social goals).
findings.matters: If the fund is diverted to non-pension purposes without funding those purposes separately, pension liabilities could become underfunded. For a lender, this signals pressure on the fund and potential conflicts between member protection and council policy.
findings.figures: Governance failure risk score: 16 (tied highest); identified in Q2 2026 risk review
findings.quote: Governance Failure (risk 11) – the potential for additional objectives over and above the paying of pensions to members being imposed on LGPS Funds has been added as a risk cause.

findings.headline: Pension fund governance responsibilities are moving from the Section 151 Officer (finance director) to a new LGPS Senior Officer position.
findings.detail: The council's constitution was updated on 21 July 2026. The new LGPS Pension Fund Sub-Committee now oversees all LGPS delivery, and key responsibilities are being moved from the Section 151 Officer (the chief finance officer) to a newly created LGPS Senior Officer position. The updated Governance Compliance Statement will take effect when this new position comes into effect.
findings.matters: For a lender assessing management capability, knowing that pension fund oversight has been separated from the chief finance officer signals either appropriate specialization or a loss of integrated financial control. The transition risk is material if the new post is not yet filled or resourced.
findings.figures: Constitution approved 21 July 2026; Governance Compliance Statement effective on date new LGPS Senior Officer role commences
findings.quote: Reflects that key responsibilities move from the Section 151 Officer to the new LGPS Senior Officer position, as set out in the Constitution updates approved by Council. The new governance compliance statement therefore will come into effect from the date that the LGPS Senior Officer position comes into effect.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation in 2028 is now the fund's highest-rated risk (score 16), adding resource pressure and governance uncertainty.
findings.detail: Warwickshire will split into two unitary authorities in 2028. The fund has added this as a new top-level risk with specific causes: inadequate resources for the required timescales, lack of consensus on the future operating model, changes in personnel and systems, clashes with the 2028 actuarial valuation, and insufficient resources to deliver both this agenda and business-as-usual LGPS work. The fund plans a project management approach and stakeholder consultation to mitigate it.
findings.matters: A pension fund split is complex and error-prone; if mismanaged, it could fracture the employer covenant or leave liabilities unmatched. The fund is already acknowledging resource constraints to deliver both the split and its ongoing obligations.
findings.figures: LGR risk score: 16 (tied highest with governance failure and climate change)
findings.quote: Following the announcement that Warwickshire will reorganise into two unitary authorities in 2028, Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) has been added as a new separate risk on the Fund's risk register. The current residual risk score is 16.

findings.paper_title: Pension Administration Activity and Performance Update
findings.headline: Regulatory rectification identifies 2,404 death cases potentially requiring recalculation and 65 cases with extra payments due
findings.detail: Following Access and Fairness regulatory changes (effective 1 April 2026), the PAS identified potentially 2,404 death cases needing recalculation and 65 cases that may involve extra death grant payments. Rectifications could span from 2005 onwards. A 12-month fixed-term Pension Officer was hired to handle this work. Costs and additional pensions owed will be funded from the Pension Fund.
findings.matters: This represents a material compliance liability triggered by regulatory change. The scale of cases needing correction (2,404) and the long lookback period (2005+) indicates systematic calculation issues. Even if individually small, this affects audit position and suggests potential future regulatory exposure.
findings.figures: 2,404 potential death cases requiring recalculation; 65 cases with possible extra death grant payments; rectification period from 2005 onwards
findings.quote: A successful recruitment campaign has been completed to hire a 12-month fixed term Pension Officer to work through the rectification cases needed on survivor benefits and death grants. The PAS has also run initial reporting on caseload to be rectified, with initial numbers showing a possible 2,404 death cases that may need recalculated and 65 cases that may involve extra death grant to be paid.

findings.paper_title: Pension Administration Activity and Performance Update
findings.headline: Key Performance Indicators show significant deterioration: only 9 of 16 met target, down from prior year across multiple areas
findings.detail: In Q1 2026, only 9 of 16 KPIs achieved the 95% target. KPI B1 (death acknowledgement) dropped to 88% from 96% prior year; B5 (deferred member pension confirmation) fell to 91% from 98%. The paper attributes this to recent staff changes and increased workload. Caseload rose 23% year-on-year (10,475 cases created vs 8,507 prior year). One new Pensions Assistant is still in training.
findings.matters: Service delivery is declining despite the council being asked to do more. The gap between current KPI performance and prior year shows the operational strain is not being absorbed, raising questions about whether staffing increases alone will restore performance.
findings.figures: 9 of 16 KPIs at target; B1 88% (was 96%); B5 91% (was 98%); 10,475 cases created April-June 2026 vs 8,507 prior year (23% increase); 2,273 open cases (down from 2,715 prior period)
findings.quote: For the period to end of June 2026, nine of the sixteen KPIs met the 95% target. Of the remaining seven, four of the KPIs were 90% or higher. The PAS has experienced a period of staff changes alongside an increase in workload, which has contributed to a reduction in performance against KPIs B1 and B5.

findings.paper_title: Pension Administration Activity and Performance Update
findings.headline: Pension Administration Service requesting 4 FTE staff increase at £168,867.60 annual cost due to benchmarking shortfall and demand growth
findings.detail: The PAS is proposing 4 additional full-time staff (15% increase) because Warwickshire has 13% less resource than comparable funds. Since 2019, scheme membership has grown 24.8% and employer numbers 31.3%. Current staffing is 26.6 FTE serving 2,258 members per FTE versus the 2,000-member benchmark. The proposal breaks down to 2 FTE for Employer Relations (1 Officer, 1 Assistant), 1 FTE for Benefits, and 1 FTE for Membership.
findings.matters: This is a material ongoing cost increase request driven by structural demand growth. Finance directors care whether service capacity matches obligations, and lenders care about councils committing to new recurring spend.
findings.figures: 4 FTE increase (15%); £134,026.92 for 3 Pension Officers; £34,840.68 for 1 Pension Assistant; total £168,867.60; current 26.6 FTE; 2,258 members per FTE vs 2,000 benchmark; 24.8% membership growth since 2019; 31.3% employer growth since 2019
findings.quote: At this time, it is proposed to increase resources within the PAS by 4 FTE, representing an increase of 15%. This will enable the team to meet BAU demand and will also facilitate the ability to innovate and take a proactive approach to service improvement.

findings.headline: Apprenticeship Levy Transfer Scheme paused indefinitely to stabilise reserves amid LGR uncertainty and future levy liabilities.
findings.detail: The council has paused its Apprenticeship Levy Transfer Scheme to 'stabilise levy reserves and protect future apprenticeship investment'. The pause is expected to remain until April 2027 and 'may need to continue until after reorganisation' due to 'uncertainty from Local Government Reorganisation and future levy liabilities'. Employer demand remains strong, but new applications cannot be progressed. This illustrates the council applying financial brakes in response to LGR uncertainty.
findings.matters: This signals the council is consciously constraining discretionary spending and managing levy liabilities cautiously ahead of reorganisation. It indicates heightened concerns about post-reorganisation financial positions and future levy responsibilities.
findings.figures: Scheme performance fell from 156% of target to 6% in Q1; pause expected until April 2027, potentially extending post-reorganisation
findings.quote: The Warwickshire County Council Apprenticeship Levy Transfer Programme has been paused to stabilise levy reserves and protect future apprenticeship investment. Given uncertainty from Local Government Reorganisation and future levy liabilities, it is expected that the pause will remain in place until April 2027 and may need to continue until after reorganisation.

findings.headline: Sickness absence has increased to 10.68 days per FTE and is at its highest level since May 2025, particularly acute in Children and Families and Social Care.
findings.detail: Sickness absence (12-month rolling average) has risen to 10.68 days per FTE in Q1, up from 10.44 in Q4, and is above the council's target of 8 days. This is 'the highest since May 2025'. The Executive Director notes there are 'very high levels of sickness in Children and Families and Social Care and Support', with only 45% of staff having had no sickness absence in the last 12 months. A comprehensive action plan is in place.
findings.matters: Elevated sickness in the council's overspent demand-facing services directly reduces operational capacity to manage existing pressures. Sickness in Children and Families (which is both overspent and facing EHCP crisis) is particularly concerning as it reduces the council's ability to close performance gaps.
findings.figures: 10.68 days per FTE (Q1, rolling 12 months, up from 10.44 Q4); target 8 days; 'very high levels' in Children and Families and Social Care; 45% of staff with zero sickness absence in last 12 months
findings.quote: after a period of stabilisation, absence had started to reduce, however over the last quarter it is increasing again and is currently at 10.68 days, the highest since May 2025.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation (creating two new councils by April 2028) will absorb significant organisational capacity at a time when the council is already stretched.
findings.detail: Warwickshire is undergoing mandatory Local Government Reorganisation with vesting date April 2028. This requires 'significant additional work associated with disaggregation' in the Resources Directorate and will impact 'the Council's capacity to deliver current priorities'. The Executive Director states performance 'will be impacted by the demands of the local government reorganisation programme'. The strategic risk register notes this creates 'capacity to deliver current priorities alongside the creation of two new councils and a fire authority by April 2028'.
findings.matters: LGR diverts senior management and finance/HR resources during a period when the council is already running overspends in major demand-facing services. This constrains the council's ability to stabilise financial pressures and reduces delivery capacity for recovery actions.
findings.figures: Vesting date April 2028 (20 months from Q1 2026/27)
findings.quote: It is likely that performance will be impacted by the demands of the local government reorganisation programme on the Resources Directorate, with significant additional work associated with disaggregation, which will require robust prioritisation and focus given the short period of time before vesting day.

findings.headline: Children and Families and Social Care and Support directorates are both overspent in Q1, offset by corporate underspends and treasury returns, requiring close monitoring.
findings.detail: The council's Q1 net outturn is 1.4% overspent (within +/-2% tolerance), but this masks directorate-level pressures. Children and Families and Social Care and Support are both running overspends; these are offset by underspends in Corporate Services and over-delivery of treasury returns. The Executive Director emphasises this 'requires very close monitoring' and notes 'concerning levels of overspend in Children and Families in particular'. Adult Social Care overspend is described as 'close to the unfunded pressure in the agreed budget'.
findings.matters: Directorate-level overspends in two major service areas indicate demand is outpacing budget allocation. Reliance on corporate underspends and treasury returns to balance the position masks structural budget pressure and is not sustainable if corporate capacity or investment returns decline.
findings.figures: 1.4% net outturn overspend (Q1), within +/-2% tolerance. Adult Social Care overspend 'close to the unfunded pressure in the agreed budget'
findings.quote: Overspends within Directorates (mainly Children and Families and Social Care and Support) are offset by underspends and over delivery of treasury returns in Corporate Services and savings through spending controls in other service areas.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit risk has been escalated to red, driven by High Needs Block overspend and uncertainty over future deficit funding before statutory override expires.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit is now flagged as a red strategic risk (residual score 16, target 9). The council's Q1 forecast notes the DSG deficit is 'significantly higher than the budgeted overspend', with the High Needs Block driving the variance. The statutory override that has allowed councils to spread deficits over future years expires, creating uncertainty over how cumulative deficits will be funded. This is treated as a material financial sustainability risk.
findings.matters: Once the override expires, uncovered DSG deficits become a direct call on the council's revenue reserves. An uncovered DSG deficit constrains financial flexibility and may force reallocation away from other services or trigger reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: DSG deficit risk residual score 16 (target 9, red rating); High Needs Block overspend 'significantly higher than the budgeted overspend'
findings.quote: The strategic risk profile has changed this quarter, with the Dedicated Schools Grant deficit risk increasing to red due to the growing in-year deficit and uncertainty over approval of the Local SEND Reform Plan and future deficit funding arrangements before the statutory override ends.

findings.headline: EHCP completion fell to 9.2% within statutory 20-week timescale in Q1, down from 19% in Q4, with 28-week average completion time
findings.detail: The council's EHCP completion performance deteriorated sharply in Q1, with only 9.2% of plans completed within the statutory 20-week timescale, compared to 19% in Q4. The council's actual average time to completion is now 28 weeks. The Executive Director calls this 'unacceptable' and 'a major concern', citing increasing demand and capacity pressures. A recovery plan is due to be completed and shared with Members.
findings.matters: This statutory service failure indicates the council is under severe structural strain in a key demand area (SEND), with capacity unable to meet legal requirements. For a lender, this signals either sustained unfunded demand growth or delivery capacity that is structurally inadequate, with reputational and financial exposure.
findings.figures: 9.2% completion within 20 weeks (Q1 2026/27, down from 19% Q4); 28-week average time to completion; national average 46%; academic year 25/26 average 18% (down from 22% prior year)
findings.quote: % Education Health Care plans completed within 20 weeks quarterly performance decreased from 19% in Quarter 4 to 9.2% in Quarter 1.

findings.headline: Phased asset disposal plan agreed from 2026/27 through Q4 2027/28 to support MTFS
findings.detail: The council has confirmed a phased asset disposal programme with explicit timeframe running through end of 2027/28. The council states this programme 'will support the current MTFS and any savings or receipts built into the MTFS refresh process.' Specific disposal values and milestones are not detailed.
findings.matters: Asset disposals are a material source of capital receipts and operating cost savings; their realisation affects MTFS delivery and medium-term cash flow. The lack of specific values raises uncertainty about financial impact.
findings.figures: No specific disposal values, quantities or phasing milestones provided
findings.quote: A phased asset disposal plan has been agreed, starting in 2026/27 through to Q4 2027/28. This programme will support the current MTFS and any savings or receipts built into the MTFS refresh process.

findings.headline: Maintenance backlog and suitability issues explicitly identified as estate challenges
findings.detail: The strategy is developed in direct response to maintenance backlog and suitability issues alongside under-utilisation of assets. These are identified as existing problems requiring structured management. The council proposes to address through phased delivery and asset rationalisation rather than new spending commitments.
findings.matters: Maintenance backlogs represent deferred investment risk and signal whether the council is actively managing asset condition or deferring costs. A lender needs visibility of the backlog scale and remediation approach.
findings.figures: No scale, cost or remediation timeline specified
findings.quote: The Strategy has been developed in response to a range of estate challenges, including maintenance backlog and suitability issues, under-utilisation, financial pressures, regulatory and compliance requirements

findings.paper_title: A Financial Framework for the 2027-32 Medium Term Financial Strategy Refresh
findings.headline: Council tax income represents 63% of corporate funding and growing; a freeze would cost £121.9m over five years (18% of current budget).
findings.detail: The council is almost entirely dependent on council tax and relies on taking the maximum 4.99% increase each year. If council tax were frozen for five years, projected income in 2031/32 would be £121.9m less than planning assumptions. The Government's funding settlement has already factored in these maximum increases, so not taking them results in a real-terms reduction in overall funding.
findings.matters: Revenue concentration risk: the council has minimal flexibility on council tax and cannot use it as a mitigating lever if other funding sources deteriorate; it is already assumed at maximum. Any resistance to council tax rises or economic slowdown in the tax base becomes an unmitigated budget pressure.

This is not presented as hypothetical; it is included as a plausible scenario for the MTFS, indicating the council expects savings delivery to fall short and is planning contingency for it.
findings.matters: Planning explicitly for 70% delivery of savings targets is an admission that achieving the full reduction is not certain; it signals that the council is managing against expected failure to deliver planned efficiencies.

findings.paper_title: A Financial Framework for the 2027-32 Medium Term Financial Strategy Refresh
findings.headline: Any 2026/27 overspend likely to increase 2027/28 savings requirement and significantly reduce reserves
findings.detail: The paper states: 'Any emerging overspend in 2026/27 is likely to increase the level of savings required in 2027/28 and future years, and significantly reduce reserves, unless mitigating action is taken.' The council is dependent on delivering £99.9m of savings over five years on top of managing current-year pressures; the framework identifies 'risks remain from rising demand increasing the costs of service delivery which may lead to in-year overspends and challenges delivering planned savings.'
findings.matters: This is explicitly flagging that the baseline assumption (current year holds, future savings are deliverable) is at risk; if 2026/27 overshoots, the council will have less cash buffer and higher required savings, creating a dual squeeze on the MTFS.
findings.figures: £99.9m savings required 2026/27–2030/31; 2026/27 Q1 monitoring expected in September will clarify position
findings.quote: Any emerging overspend in 2026/27 is likely to increase the level of savings required in 2027/28 and future years, and significantly reduce reserves, unless mitigating action is taken.

findings.paper_title: A Financial Framework for the 2027-32 Medium Term Financial Strategy Refresh
findings.headline: Pay inflation is already expected to exceed budget; the council has offered 3.3% but anticipates actual costs will be higher.
findings.detail: The council set aside 3.0% pay inflation in the 2026/27 budget and offered 3.3% to staff, but already estimates that 2026/27 pay inflation 'will exceed the 3.3% offered by the National Joint Council. Without any wider change to improve the Council's market position in terms of pay and reward, this cannot be contained.' This suggests the council is already facing cost pressures beyond budget in its largest controllable cost area.
findings.matters: Pay overrun is a leading indicator of budget control failure; if the council cannot contain labour costs (which represent a large portion of social care and other controllable spending), this signals either weak cost management or unmanageable service cost growth.
findings.figures: 3.0% provision in budget; 3.3% offered to staff; actual expected to exceed both
findings.quote: basic pay inflation in 2026/27 will exceed the 3.3% offered by the National Joint Council. Without any wider change to improve the Council's market position in terms of pay and reward, this cannot be contained within the 3.0% provision set aside in the 2026/27 MTFS

findings.paper_title: A Financial Framework for the 2027-32 Medium Term Financial Strategy Refresh
findings.headline: The DSG High Needs statutory override ends on 31 March 2028, at which point the council must find a sustainable solution for an accumulated cumulative deficit.
findings.detail: The council is currently using balance sheet resources to manage the cashflow impact of the DSG High Needs deficit while the statutory override is in place. The paper flags that a 'sustainable national solution' is needed after March 2028 but makes no assumption of what that will be; it is planning on the basis that the deficit will somehow be resolved. Until then, the council is using reserves to manage the deficit and is dependent on an unconfirmed High Needs Stability Grant.
findings.matters: A structural deficit in a ringfenced grant that sits outside the council's control, funded by drawing down general reserves until a government solution materialises, is a material off-balance-sheet liability for a lender assessing financial position.
findings.figures: Override expires 31 March 2028; cumulative deficits managed through balance sheet through that date
findings.quote: managing the cumulative DSG High Needs deficit position and responding to the prolonged budgetary and cashflow challenges arising from the growing cumulative deficit until the end of the Statutory Override on 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: A Financial Framework for the 2027-32 Medium Term Financial Strategy Refresh
findings.headline: The Department of Education has confirmed zero Basic Need grant funding for school places to 2027/28 with no indication of future funding.
findings.detail: The council has a statutory duty to provide school places but will not receive grant funding from central government. This means the council must either fund growth from its own budget, defer provision, or halt capital projects. The paper describes this as 'a step change' in capital pressures and signals that prioritisation will result in approval only for 'unavoidable' projects or those delivering 'greatest benefits'.
findings.matters: A statutory obligation with zero dedicated funding creates a structural budget pressure that will require either capital borrowing or diversion of other capital resources; for a lender, this signals ongoing pressure on the capital strategy and cash flow.
findings.figures: Zero funding confirmed to 2027/28; Department of Education has given no indication of future funding
findings.quote: the risk to the funding of the provision for new school places with the Department of Education having confirmed zero Basic Need grant funding for Warwickshire up to 2027/28 and no indication of funding in future years.

findings.paper_title: A Financial Framework for the 2027-32 Medium Term Financial Strategy Refresh
findings.headline: £6.2m of social care costs are not funded in the current budget and must be absorbed through contingency reserves.
findings.detail: Adults and Children's Social Care have £6.2m of unfunded pressures that were identified in the 2026/27 s.25 statement. The council plans to manage anything beyond this through spending controls and the Short-Term Financial Risk Reserve. However, initial forecasts suggest 2026/27 will see 'continuing, significant pressures' in these high-demand areas, which could exceed the contingency and force further savings in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Unfunded social care spending in the current year is a concrete budget leak; a lender evaluating the council's financial control would flag this as evidence of either unrealistic budgeting or cost growth the council cannot manage.
findings.figures: £6.2m unfunded; total 2026/27 budget £702.3m
findings.quote: £6.2m of pressures in children's and adult social care (as outlined in the 2026/27 s.25 statement accompanying the budget resolution) were not fully funded in the agreed budget and MTFS.

findings.matters: Major local government restructuring creates transition risks and costs; lenders need visibility on the scope, timeline, financial impact and whether this is mandatory or discretionary reorganisation.

This represents significant acceleration in capital financing provision for schools, though the reserve name suggests these are short-term financing costs rather than capital values.
findings.matters: Growing school capital financing costs indicate increased capital commitments or deferred costs materializing, both of which affect future borrowing needs and budget priorities that lenders monitor.

findings.headline: Short-term financial risk contingency reserve increased by £10m to £22.4m
findings.detail: The Short-Term Financial Risk Reserve increased from 12,394k to 22,408k, an increase of 10,014k in the year. The council notes that this reserve is "used to balance out service overspends and is not available for allocation", indicating it is held specifically for managing unexpected service pressures.
findings.matters: Significant increases in contingency reserves indicate the council anticipates financial pressures or service delivery risks; this scale of increase suggests the council is bracing for tighter financial conditions.
findings.figures: 12,394k (opening) to 22,408k (closing), increase of 10,014k

findings.matters: Volatility reserves allow councils to absorb unexpected income shocks; their exhaustion signals significantly reduced financial shock absorption capacity and leaves the council exposed to income variations.

findings.headline: Children's internal legal fees overspent £0.790m (up £0.725m on prior year) due to case volume and duration
findings.detail: Legal recharge for 2025-26 is £0.725m more than 2024-25, reflecting an ongoing increase in the number of cases and placements the service is dealing with. This is a pass-through cost that rises automatically with case demand and suggests the Children's service is handling materially more complex, contested cases.
findings.matters: Legal costs are a trailing indicator of case complexity and contested proceedings; a 48% year-on-year increase (£0.725m on baseline of ~£1.5m) suggests systemic increase in case difficulty or challenge.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - P12 25-26 Commentary on revenue outturn variances
findings.headline: Parent & Baby residential placements jumped unexpectedly to £0.929m overspend after MTFS savings were actioned
findings.detail: A MTFS budget saving had been actioned against Parent & Baby placements based on historical trend, but the service experienced a dramatic, unexpected increase in activity. Weekly costs rose 42% from £5,151 (2024-25) to £7,331 (2025-26), driven by higher-than-expected Children in Care who are pregnant and rapid cost escalation. The council had cut the budget in anticipation of lower demand, then saw demand spike.
findings.matters: Forecasting failure: the council removed a savings line expecting lower demand, then demand rose 42%. Signals poor forecast linkage between social care demand and maternity services.
findings.figures: £0.929m overspend (P10 £0.850m, Q3 £0.600m); Weekly cost rise: £5,151 → £7,331 (+42%); MTFS saving actioned against this budget before demand spike
findings.quote: This financial year has seen activity levels dramatically increase which was an unexpected upturn in trend based on previous years, (indeed, an MTFS budget saving was actioned against this budget in 2025-26). The final position is an overspend of £0.929m (P10 £0.850m, Q3 £0.600m) The main reason for the increase in activity is a higher-than-expected increase of Children in Care who are pregnant coupled with the weekly average costs increasing at a fast rate, rising from £5,666 at Q1, to £6,280 at Q2, to £6,910 at P10 to a final rate of £7,331 for 2025-26. In comparison the 2024-25 rate was £5,151 per week.

findings.headline: Warwickshire Property and Development Group £2.457m commercial shortfall covered from Commercial Risk Reserve
findings.detail: The commercial property vehicle missed its £2.741m net income target by £2.457m, requiring drawdown from the Commercial Risk Reserve. Council states 'future years' returns expected to replenish the reserve,' but no detail on how shortfall will be recovered or whether business plan assumptions need revision.
findings.matters: A material miss on commercial vehicle income (90% of target) signals either optimistic business planning or deteriorating property market conditions. Replenishment reliance is concerning if reserve depletion continues.
findings.figures: £2.457m shortfall (target £2.741m, achieved £0.284m); Covered from Commercial Risk Reserve; £0.300m Scape Dividend to partially replenish reserve
